text: 13 (Rectal diazepam may also have a role in this setting to treat acute repeti- tive seizures,14 which may evolve into status epilepti- cus.) Both midazolam15,16 and lorazepam17 have also been given intranasally • For sustained control in patients with established epilep- sy their usual antiepileptic regimen may be given orally or by nasogastric tube once immediate control is estab- lished, or if necessary, for those drugs with an intrave- nous formulation, parenterally.4,5 • In other patients, or in patients with established status not abolished by the benzodiazepine, additional treat- ment with one of several first-line antiepileptics is nor- mally required. The choice is usually between intrave- nous phenytoin, fosphenytoin, or phenobarbital,3-5,7,8 all of which are effective. Repeat doses may need to be giv- en. Although there is some evidence that phenobarbital is more effective than phenytoin in abolishing sei- zures,18 many favour the use of the barbiturate only in patients who do not respond to phenytoin or fospheny- toin,1-3,9,10 because of the risk of severe respiratory de- pression. ECG monitoring is required in patients given intravenous phenytoin or fosphenytoin.4 • Other antiepileptics have been used for established sta- tus. Some have found intravenous valproate to be useful in this situation,7,19-21 and have incorporated it into local protocols. Other alternatives have included paraldehyde rectally or by deep intramuscular injection, and intrave- nous clomethiazole edisilate was formerly available. The BNF notes that rectal paraldehyde causes little 470 Antiepileptics respiratory depression and may therefore be useful where facilities for resuscitation are poor. Another op- tion is to give lidocaine intravenously.3 Pyridoxine may be tried in children under 3 years of age with established convulsive status epilepticus, in case the seizures are py- ridoxine dependent or responsive.1 • Once seizures have continued for 60 to 90 minutes de- spite treatment with a benzodiazepine and one of the first-line antiepileptics, the patient is considered to have refractory status epilepticus.3,5 At this point general anaesthesia should be instituted. The usual choice is be- tween treatment with propofol, midazolam, or a short- acting barbiturate anaesthetic such as pentobarbital or thiopental.3-10,22 The anaesthetic should be continued for 12 to 24 hours after the last clinical or electrographic seizure and the dose then gradually reduced.5 Some con- sider that all patients unresponsive to first-line therapy with a benzodiazepine should be considered refractory and proceed to treatment with propofol or midazolam.6 • Other drugs tried in refractory status include the inhala- tional anaesthetic
